Project Overview

Research Viewer is a local-first research application designed to handle very large document and image archives in a structured, reliable, and privacy-preserving way. The system was built to support long-term academic and archival research, where users need to browse thousands of scanned documents, annotate them, bookmark important pages, and organize material into collections — all without relying on cloud services.
The application is optimized for serious research workflows, not public-facing access, and prioritizes data ownership, performance, and offline reliability.
Problem This System Solves
Researchers working with large archival collections often face challenges such as:

items: Massive document volumes (thousands of high-resolution images)
Poor organization and slow navigation
Lack of persistent annotations and bookmarks
Dependence on cloud tools that compromise privacy or performance
Difficulty collaborating without duplicating data

blocks.text: Research Viewer addresses these issues by providing a self-contained, offline-capable system that keeps all data local while still supporting structured research workflows and optional collaboration.
System Design & Architecture
The system follows a local-first architecture, meaning all data lives on the user’s machine.
Core Components

items: Local Backend Service: Handles data access, authentication, and coordination between UI and storage.
Web-Based Frontend UI: Used for browsing, viewing, annotating, and organizing documents. — Can be accessed via: — A standard browser (local) — A desktop wrapper (Electron)
Local Storage Layer: SQLite database for metadata and user-generated data — Large image archive stored directly on disk (not duplicated)

blocks.text: No cloud services, remote databases, or third-party storage are required
Archive & Data Model
The system is designed around a hierarchical archival structure, reflecting real-world research collections:
Series → Reels → Items → Images

items: Items are the primary research unit
Each item may contain hundreds or thousands of images
All annotations, bookmarks, and collections operate at the image and item level

blocks.text: This structure allows efficient navigation while preserving archival context
Key Features
High-Performance Document Viewer

items: Large image viewing with zoom and pan
Page-level navigation for long documents
Full-screen viewing for detailed analysis

blocks.text: Annotations

items: Region-based annotations (highlight specific areas)
Image-level note annotations
Persistent and user-specific
Synced across different viewing modes.

blocks.text: Bookmarks

items: Save and return to exact document pages
Metadata-aware (series, reel, item, page)
Designed for long research sessions

blocks.text: Collections

items: Group images from different documents into custom collections
Enables thematic research without altering the archive structure
Separate “Collection Viewer” for focused review

blocks.text: Search & Navigation

items: Structured search across series, reels, and items
Designed for fast discovery, not full-text analysis
Built to scale with large archival datasets

blocks.text: Security & Data Ownership

items: All data stored locally
User accounts managed by the application
No external authentication providers
Optional, temporary multi-user access via secure tunneling (operator-controlled)
No data leaves the host system unless explicitly enabled.

blocks.text: This makes the system suitable for sensitive archives and institutional research environments.
Scale & Real-World Use

items: Designed to handle large, high-resolution archival collections
Supports thousands of images per item
Optimized for long-running research sessions
Built for historians, archivists, and academic researcher

Project Overview

The OBD-II Based Auto Dynamics System is a compact, cost-effective vehicle diagnostics and performance analysis platform designed for rally and high-performance vehicles. The project was built as a team effort to bridge the gap between basic OBD-II scanners and expensive motorsport telemetry systems.
The system collects vehicle diagnostics and motion data, performs on-device anomaly detection using TinyML, and provides real-time and post-race analytics through a mobile app and a cloud dashboard.
Problem This Project Addresses

Standard OBD-II tools provide limited insight into real-time vehicle dynamics, while professional motorsport telemetry systems are costly and difficult to customize. Our goal was to design a portable, intelligent, and affordable alternative that:

items: Works offline by default
Supports real-time diagnostics
Adds intelligence through edge-based ML
Enables flexible visualization without vendor lock-in

Edge Processing: Embedded processing on Arduino Nano ESP32-S3 — On-device anomaly detection using TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers
Wireless Communication: Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) for live data streaming to a mobile app — Wi-Fi + MQTT for cloud uploads when triggered by the user
Visualization & Analytics: Mobile app for real-time monitoring — Cloud-hosted dashboard for post-race analysis

blocks.text: Large-Scale Web Scraping & Metadata Processing Pipeline
Project Overview
This project involved building a large-scale, production-grade data pipeline to harvest, structure, and download the complete William Howard Taft Papers collection from the Library of Congress.

The collection contains hundreds of thousands of high-resolution archival images with complex metadata relationships. The core challenge was not scraping alone, but designing a system that is reliable, resumable, auditable, and scalable enough to run continuously over long periods without data loss or duplication.
The final system produces clean relational datasets (CSV + SQLite) and a robust bulk image downloader, forming a foundation for future research, OCR, annotation, and AI-based analysis.
Scale & Complexity

items: Hundreds of reels and cataloged items
~770,000 cataloged images (JPG + TIFF variants)
~1.5 million total files
Expected dataset size: 15–20 TB
Long-running downloads spanning weeks, not hours

blocks.text: This required careful attention to filesystem limits, network reliability, metadata consistency, and recovery from partial failures.
What the System Does
Metadata Harvesting & Structuring

items: Extracts structured metadata from the Library of Congress APIs
Preserves raw JSON snapshots for traceability
Normalizes metadata into relational tables (series, reels, items, subjects, headings)
Uses consistent identifiers to maintain clean relationships across all data

blocks.text: Image Inventory

items: Builds a complete inventory of all cataloged images
Tracks page-level details including item ID, reel ID, and frame numbers
Reconciles differences between public image counts and officially cataloged metadata
Produces a verifiable, auditable record of what exists and what does not

blocks.text: Bulk Image Downloading

items: Downloads highest-resolution JPG and TIFF images
Uses polite rate limiting and retry logic
Fully resume-safe: interrupted runs continue without re-downloading verified files
Maintains a persistent index tracking status, size, attempts, and errors
Designed to run unattended for long durations

blocks.text: Relational Database Design

items: Builds a SQLite database linking all metadata tables
Images remain as normal files on disk; the database stores references
Deterministic filenames embed identifiers, making files self-describing
Enables future tooling to retrieve metadata and images together efficiently

blocks.text: Key Design Decisions
Deterministic Filenames
Each image filename encodes its identifiers (series, reel, item, page), ensuring:

items: Files are traceable even without the database
Relationships remain intact across systems
Storage layout can change without breaking references

blocks.text: Database + Filesystem Separation

items: Metadata lives in SQLite for fast querying
Large binary files stay on disk for efficiency
This avoids database bloat while keeping relationships explicit

blocks.text: Resume & Audit Safety

items: No file is downloaded twice once verified
Failed or missing files are logged explicitly
Index rebuild allows recovery even if runtime state is lost
Designed for imperfect networks and real-world interruptions

blocks.text: Building My Own 8-Bit CPU: A Hardware Adventure
So, I decided to make my own 8-bit CPU. It's like a tiny brain that can follow 16 different commands. Let me break down how I put it together!

First of all, I was supposed to make the individual components of the datapath, and then group them together into a single file of datapath. The individual components included the multiplexer, arithmetic logic unit, register file, tri-state-buffer and accumulator. The explanation of each of the components is given below. Initially, I tested each of the components separately, and then I did a combined test of all the components together in the datapath file.

The datapath starts with the multiplexer, and depending on the mux select value, it passes the appropriate value to the accumulator. When the acc_write control signal is ‘1’, it reads and stores the output of the multiplexer. After that, the value of the accumulator can go to three possible components. First, it can go to the register file to write/store a value in one of the 8 registers. Second, it goes to the ALU and acts as one of the inputs for the ALU. Third, it also goes to the tri-state buffer, where depending on the control signal ‘output_enable’, it stores the value in the buffer and then further displays it on the seven-segment display.
Step 1: Creating the Core (DataPath)
Multiplexer Madness

The multiplexer chooses from four 8-bit inputs, determining which one gets written to the accumulator based on the specifications outlined in Table 2. There were 4 possible inputs to the multiplexer, namely ALU output, register file output, immediate data and the user input.’
Registers: The Memory Keepers

The register entity consists of 8 registers each of width 8 bits, which makes a total of 8*8 = 64 bits storage in total. Since there are 8 registers, we need only 3 bits to determine the address of a specific register. There’s also a write enable signal, which decides whether to read or write in the registers.
ALU: Arithmetic Wizardry

The role of the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) is to perform arithmetic and logic operations on the data. It receives input from the register file and accumulator, which is then processed according to the instruction provided by the program, and then sends the results back for further use or storage. The ALU designed in lab 3, consisted of a total of 8 operations, which are shown in the table below. There were 3 bits dedicated for the alu select, and 2 bits to determine the value of bits_rotate.
Tri-State Buffer

The tri-state buffer consists of an enable signal, and when activated, it directs the content of the accumulator to be stored in the buffer. This buffered information is then showcased to the user through the two-digit seven-segment LED display, serving as the CPU's output.
Accumulator: The Heartbeat

The accumulator is an essential 8-bit register which plays an important role in the overall system by working as a bridge between the multiplexer and the other components of the datapath. The output of the accumulator is distributed to three key components. Firstly, it contributes data to the register file. Secondly, it serves as an input for the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU). Lastly, the accumulator's output also goes into the tri-state buffer, enabling the display of CPU’s output to the user on the two-digit seven-segment LED display.

Combining these elements births the DataPath, the computational core where the magic unfolds. Simulating the DataPath validates the synergy of its components, setting the stage for the CPU's grand performance.

Datapath is the hardware that performs all the data processing and the required operations, for example, ALU, registers, and internal buses. It consists of all the 5 individual components, namely ALU, multiplexer, Register file, accumulator and tri-state buffer. In the datapath file, we instantiate all the components and link the signals and ports as required by the design
Step 2: Crafting the Controller

In next part, I was supposed to complete the design of the controller module, which is the brain of the whole CPU. Here, I defined different states in the finite state machine, one for each instruction (except CSKIP, it takes 2 clock cycles), one for STATE FETCH and one for STATE DECODE.

Firstly, the state machine fetches the instruction from the program memory and then decodes it in the next clock cycle. Now, after determining the opcode of the instruction, the state machine accordingly goes to the next state. After the execution of the instruction is over, the state machine again goes to the STATE FETCH to fetch the next instruction, and the whole cycle keeps on repeating.

So, the controller sends the required control signals to the datapath module, which then completes the execution of the instruction. There are a total of 15 instructions in the instruction set architecture, out of which, 13 were given to us in the manual and we were required to implement the rest of the 2 instructions. The two custom instructions, which we are using are JMPR and CSKIP. Below, we have described the implementation of both the instructions in detail.
JMPR (Jump Relative)

This instruction does a memory jump in the program. If we want to skip ahead, then use a positive number; if we need to go back, then use a negative number. We use 6 bits for this, where the first bit decides the direction (plus or minus), and the other 5 bits tell us how far to jump, allowing for a range from -32 to 31 in the memory shift.
CSKIP (Conditional SKIP)

CSKIP instruction skips the next instruction if the accumulator equals the value in register R[rrr], which is specified in the instruction binary code. Note that, CSKIP skips the entire next instruction, irrespective of its size; for instance, even if the instruction is 16 bits, the entire instruction is bypassed instead of just skipping one memory location of 8 bits. In the CSKIP instruction, we examined the opcodes of the next instruction. If the next instruction was 16 bits, we advanced by 2 memory locations; for 8-bit instructions, we skipped just one memory location.
Step 3: Combining the Datapath and the Controller

Next I completed the cpu_core design file, which instantiated datapath and controller entities. So, cpu_core acts like a top level entity for datapath and controller. Then I finished the cpu core testbench and cpu core constraint files.

I defined ‘user_input’ and ‘enter’ values in the cpu core testbench. Unlike other testbench files the test program is defined in the controller design file. Therefore, I only need two inputs: user input only if user input is required by a program defined in controller entity and enter value which is required to translate from one state to another.

At last, I created a top level entity, named “cpu_interface”, where I instantiated the cpu_core entity and the rest of the code was already instantiated. The other entity instantiations included SSD_Driver, keypad_detector, keypad_register and output_control. In the constraint file, I mapped all the output and input ports defined in the top level interface entity.
Custom Program: Single Product Inventory Manager

Our custom program is a Single Product Inventory Management System which stores the current and updated values of the inventory. Our program utilizes all 32 program memory spaces from PM(0) to PM(31), and also includes the custom instructions, namely CSKIP and JMPR.

items: User have to provide input at 9th instruction to choose add/sub (0 for sub and 1 for add).
Next the user have to provide the input 15th (0F) instruction (Number of items to add)
Next the user have to provide the input 21st (15) instruction (Number of items to sub)
Next the user have to provide the input 27th (1B) instruction (0 to continue)

blocks.text: The following registers are getting used in the program and their role is mentioned below -:

items: Register 0 → Totals items while initialization
Register 1 → No. of items to Add
Register 2 → No. of items to remove
Register 5 → Initialized with 1
Register 7 → Updated inventory value

blocks.text: Project Overview

This project involved building a navigation-style system that computes the shortest path between two locations on a real-world road network. Using the Edmonton city road dataset, the system allows a user to select two geographic points and returns the shortest route between them.
The core of the project is a graph-based pathfinding engine implemented in C++, designed to work efficiently on a large road network.
What the System Does

items: Loads a real-world road network graph of Edmonton
Converts geographic coordinates (latitude/longitude) into graph vertices
Finds the nearest road nodes to user-selected start and end points
Computes the shortest path between those nodes using Dijkstra’s algorithm
Outputs the path step-by-step using a simple server-style protocol

blocks.text: Key Concepts & Techniques

items: Graph representation using weighted directed graphs
Dijkstra’s algorithm implemented with a priority queue (min-heap)
Manhattan distance used as edge weights based on geographic coordinates
Efficient nearest-vertex lookup for mapping real locations to graph nodes
Clean separation between graph logic, pathfinding, and I/O handling

Work with large graphs and performance-sensitive code
Translate geographic data into usable computational structures
Design modular C++ systems with clear responsibilities

elevator-project.title: Elevator Control System on Zybo Z7

blocks.text: Crafting an Elevator System with VHDL on Zybo Z7

This project focuses on designing and implementing digital systems using VHDL and finite state machines (FSMs) on the Zybo Z7 FPGA board. The work was divided into three main parts, gradually moving from pattern detection to a fully functional elevator controller with safety handling and testing.
Part 1: Binary Pattern Detection (00XX1) Using a Moore FSM

In the first phase, I implemented a Moore finite state machine in VHDL to detect a specific binary sequence (00XX1). The goal was to understand how FSMs behave in real hardware and how state transitions respond to sequential input data.

items: Implemented the FSM in VHDL
Deployed and tested it on the Zybo Z7 board
Verified detection using LED outputs
Gained hands-on experience with clock-driven state transitions

blocks.text: Part 2: Analyzing the “Sequence Spectrum” Black Box

In the second phase, I worked with a pre-built module called SequenceSpectrum provided by CircuitWorks. The challenge was to treat it as a black box and understand its behavior by analyzing inputs and outputs.
Inputs

items: Clock (K17): Drives the system
Data_in (G15 / SW0): Binary input stream
Clock Button (K18 / BTN0): Manual clock trigger

blocks.text: Outputs

items: Data Display (M14 / LD0): Processed data output
LED Indicators (LD1–LD3): State and pattern indicators
Sequence Detected (F17 / LD6): Signals successful detection

blocks.text: This phase strengthened my understanding of signal timing, hardware debugging, and FSM behavior without access to internal logic.
Part 3: Elevator Controller System on FPGA
In the final phase, I designed a 4-floor elevator controller using VHDL. The system handled floor transitions, emergency conditions, and real-time status display.
Features

items: 4-floor elevator logic
Emergency handling with a 20-second wait state
Floor status and movement indicators
Fully clock-driven FSM design

blocks.text: One of the main challenges was implementing accurate time delays using clock frequency calculations, especially for the emergency wait condition.
Testing & Validation
A dedicated testbench was created to validate the elevator controller:

items: Verified emergency response behavior
Tested upward movement (0 → 1 → 2 → 3)
Tested downward movement (3 → 2 → 1 → 0)
Confirmed correct state transitions under all scenarios

blocks.text: This ensured the system behaved reliably in both normal and edge cases.
Key Learnings

items: Practical use of VHDL and FSMs
Hardware-based debugging on FPGA
Clock management and timing constraints
Designing reliable digital systems with safety logic

blocks.text: This project helped build a strong foundation in digital design and FPGA-based system development, and it reinforced how structured state machines can be used to model real-world systems effectively.

research-intern.title: Monte Carlo Simulation of Ionic Devices

blocks.text: Ionic Devices Applicability in the Ising Model

In nanotechnology, controlling local ion transport and electrochemical reactions is extremely important. Ionic devices, made possible by advances in this field, show unique behavior and can compete with traditional semiconductor devices in terms of speed. This work explores how ionic devices behave when modeled using the Ising framework, focusing on migration probability, nanostructure effects, and magnetization behavior.
Migration Probability in Ionic Devices

Migration probability determines how easily ions move inside an ionic device. This directly affects how fast and efficient the device operates. Higher migration probability usually results in quicker responses and better performance, making it an important factor when studying ionic devices.
Nanostructure Factor in Ionic Devices

The nanostructure of an ionic device strongly influences its physical behavior. It affects interaction strength between spins and the overall stability of the system. Devices with higher nanostructure factors often show more complex and enhanced behavior compared to those with lower values. Understanding this factor helps improve the design and performance of ionic devices.
Experimental Setup and Methodology

To study these effects, simulations were performed using a grid with randomly distributed lithium spins and doping configurations. The Metropolis algorithm was used to calculate energy changes, update spins, and explore the energy landscape. This approach allows detailed analysis of ion transport and electrochemical behavior in ionic devices.
Metropolis Algorithm in Detail

The Metropolis algorithm works step by step. First, energy changes are calculated. Then, spin updates are accepted or rejected based on temperature and probability. Over time, the system evolves toward equilibrium. This method provides a reliable way to study how ions behave inside a lattice.
Understanding the Ising Model

The Ising model is a well-known framework used to study magnetic systems arranged on a grid. It helps explain how spins interact with each other and how temperature affects magnetization. Beyond magnetism, the Ising model has also been applied to neural networks, optimization problems, and social systems.
Magnetization Behavior in Ionic Devices

In an ideal system, magnetization decreases as temperature increases, eventually approaching zero as the material transitions from a ferromagnetic to a paramagnetic state. However, in ionic devices, magnetization does not follow this clear trend. Instead, it appears random, with no dominant direction. This suggests that ionic systems may not fully follow traditional Ising model behavior.
Results and Analysis

The results show how average magnetization changes with temperature for both ideal and ionic systems. Differences between the two cases highlight the impact of noise, lattice size, and ion dynamics. Susceptibility trends also show irregular behavior in ionic systems, making analysis more challenging.
Energy Landscape Comparison

The energy landscape of ionic devices contains many local minima, indicating a complex system with multiple metastable states. This makes control and prediction more difficult. In contrast, the ideal system has fewer minima, making it easier to analyze and stabilize.
Discussion on Relaxation Times

Relaxation time comparisons show how long the system takes to reach a stable state. Lower values indicate faster convergence. The ideal case converges more quickly, while the ionic case shows slower and more variable behavior, likely due to doping and ion movement.
Future Possibilities in Ionic Devices

Although current results suggest that ionic devices do not perfectly fit the Ising model, some simulations show promising behavior. With further improvements and modifications, ionic devices may better align with Ising-based modeling. Continued research could open new applications and deeper understanding.
Conclusion

This study examines how ionic devices behave within the Ising model framework. While several challenges remain, the results highlight areas where improvements are possible. Future work may improve compatibility and unlock new opportunities for ionic devices in nanotechnology and computational modeling.

blocks.text: Controlling a Stepper Motor Using the Zybo Z7

During the Winter 2023 term, as part of the ECE 315 – Computer Interfacing course, this project focused on gaining hands-on experience with embedded systems by controlling a stepper motor using the Zybo Z7 development board running the FreeRTOS real-time operating system.
The main goals of the project were to improve the user interface for stepper motor control and to experimentally measure the speed and acceleration limits of a small stepper motor.
Hardware Used
The following hardware components were used in this project:

items: Zybo Z7 Development Board: Digilent Zybo Z7 board featuring the Zynq-7000 SoC and running the FreeRTOS real-time kernel.
28BYJ-48 Stepper Motor: A small stepper motor with unipolar drive windings.
ULN2003 Driver Module: Used to drive the stepper motor coils safely and efficiently.
LTV-847 Opto-Isolator Transistor Array: Implemented to isolate and protect sensitive digital components from voltage spikes.
Resistors and Wiring: Used to assemble the opto-isolation circuit on a breadboard.

blocks.text: References and Documentation
The project relied on multiple technical references, including:

items: Digilent Zybo Z7 Reference Manual
FreeRTOS Reference Manual
ECE 315 course lecture slides
Datasheets for the stepper motor, ULN2003 IC, and LTV-847 opto-isolator

blocks.text: Hardware Setup

Before development began, the hardware setup was assembled and verified. This included removing the 7-segment LED Pmod from the Zybo Z7 board and building the opto-isolation circuit on a breadboard to ensure safe motor control.
Provided Stepper Motor Control Software
An initial software framework was provided, featuring:

items: A FreeRTOS task that communicated with the user via UART
A user interface allowing control over:: Current motor position — Speed — Acceleration and deceleration — Destination position — Dwell time

blocks.text: A library of stepper motor functions was also provided, including initialization, parameter configuration, motion control, motion status checking, and motor shutdown.
Exercise 1: FreeRTOS Task Completion

The first task involved completing the _Task_Motor() FreeRTOS task, which controls stepper motor movement based on user-defined parameters. The RGB LED on the Zybo Z7 board was used to visually indicate the motor’s operating state.
Exercise 2: Emergency Stop Implementation
An emergency stop feature was implemented using the Zybo Z7 pushbutton (BTN0). When triggered:

items: Motor operation stopped immediately
The RGB LED blinked red to indicate the emergency state

blocks.text: This feature added an important safety mechanism to the motor control system.
Key Learnings
This project provided practical experience in:

items: Hardware interfacing and protection using opto-isolation
Real-time task management with FreeRTOS
UART-based user interface design
Stepper motor control and performance evaluation
Implementing safety features in embedded systems

blocks.text: The successful completion of the project demonstrated a solid understanding of real-time embedded systems, hardware-software integration, and motor control concepts covered in the ECE 315 course.
